display_title: New Rail Route From Malmö To Oslo
short_summary: A new direct train service connects Malmö, Sweden, to Oslo, Norway, offering travelers a scenic journey along the western coast with stops in Varberg and Gothenburg.

sources.name: The Guardian
sources.title: Saunas, cinnamon buns and coastal scenery on the new rail route from Malmö to Oslo

paragraphs: A new direct rail connection now links the far south of Sweden with the Norwegian capital in roughly six and a half hours. Operated by Snälltåget, the service travels along Sweden's picturesque western corridor, providing an affordable and convenient alternative to previous routes that required long bus rides and multiple fragmented train transfers. Tickets start at around £11 each way, and the line has already proved to be an instant hit, shuttling more than 25,000 passengers since its summer launch. Operating just one direct daily departure from Malmö Central at 6:38 AM, the train offers a delightfully nostalgic atmosphere inside its iconic red-shelled dining carriage, which comes complete with the aroma of strong filter coffee and freshly baked cinnamon buns.

Travelers taking advantage of this new route can make several enriching stops along Sweden's western shore. The southern port city of Malmö, situated just across the Øresund Bridge from Copenhagen, offers a youthful, gritty, and multicultural atmosphere. Nearly half of its population is under thirty-five, and an impressive 187 nationalities are represented, fostering a vibrant creative scene. Cultural hubs include the Form/Design Center—housed in a former sixteenth-century grain store—along with the Moderna Museet and Malmö Konsthall art galleries. Neighborhoods like Möllevången, affectionately known as Möllan, buzz with local energy, organic wine bars, and trendy eateries where patrons look as though they have just returned from an art college weekend in Berlin.

Continuing north past the romanesque towers of Lund Cathedral and flat agricultural fields, the train reaches Varberg, a historic spa town reminiscent of a coastal British market town complete with cobbled streets and a weekend market. Varberg is famous for its pretty, Moorish-inspired Kallbadhuset, a cold bath house built on wooden piles above the Kattegat sea. For about £8, visitors can enjoy segregated nude saunas and a brisk plunge into the brisk water, following a tradition of nude bathing that has existed here for over a century. For further unique culture, Hotell Gästis features an unusual subterranean spa modeled after Vladimir Lenin's favorite St Petersburg bathhouse, constructed by eccentric local entrepreneur Lasse Diding as a homage to his communist ideals.

A short thirty-nine-minute fast train ride brings passengers onward to Gothenburg, Sweden's second-largest city. Known for its compact, easy-going nature and liveability, Gothenburg boasts vibrant shopping districts on Kungsgatan, vintage boutiques like Ragtime and Pop, and craft stores on Magasingatan. Visitors can indulge in a traditional fika at the multi-story Da Matteo cafe, which roasts its own coffee and bakes fresh cardamom buns in an industrial-chic setting. The city also features charming historic quarters like Haga, with its narrow cobbled streets and wooden trams, alongside Slottsskogen, an expansive park comparable in size to Hyde Park that houses deer, penguins, and Gotland ponies.

The final leg of the journey from Gothenburg to Oslo serves as a cinematic climax. Passengers gaze out the window at rolling green pastures, thick conifer forests, widening lakes, and increasingly grand granite canyons. Upon arrival in Oslo, visitors can stay at the minimalist Citybox hotel and take a short trip to the outskirts for a hike up Vettakollen. Reaching the rocky viewpoint rewards hikers with a stunning perspective where the urban sprawl of metal and glass meets the serene waters of the fjord, perfectly illustrating the seamless blend of urban and natural worlds in Scandinavia.

facts.fact: A new direct train service operated by Snälltåget connects Malmö in southern Sweden to the Norwegian capital of Oslo in just over six hours.
The route has transported more than 25,000 passengers since launching in the summer, with one-way tickets starting at £11.
Stops along the western corridor include the seaside town of Varberg and the lively city of Gothenburg.
Varberg features the Moorish-inspired Kallbadhuset cold bath house on wooden piles above the Kattegat sea.
Hotell Gästis in Varberg houses a replica of Vladimir Lenin's favorite bathhouse created by owner Lasse Diding.
Gothenburg offers attractions such as Hotel Pigalle, the Da Matteo cafe, and Slottsskogen park.
Travelers arriving in Oslo can hike up to Vettakollen for panoramic views of the city and fjord.
